question: Does this survey provide a comprehensive, technically reliable, and reproducible account of how deep neural networks solve PDEs, and do its taxonomy and efficiency claims remain useful against the literature available through 2026-08-24?

key_findings.claim: The survey's clearest contribution is an accessible historical split between instance-specific physics-constrained networks and data-trained neural operators, connected to application areas and early approximation theory.
key_findings.evidence: The paper follows Hopfield-style neural minimization, function and functional approximation, Lagaris-style trial solutions, PINNs, DeepONet, and FNO. Tables 1-3 cross the two principal families with theory, single-physics modeling, engineering and medical applications, inverse problems, and future directions. This is useful as a 2022 orientation map even though it is not a complete taxonomy of neural PDE computation.

key_findings.claim: The paper calls itself comprehensive but does not report a systematic-review method that would make its 222-reference corpus complete, auditable, or reproducible.
key_findings.evidence: The survey says it reviews work from 1982 through 2022 and presents collected references in three tables, but gives no databases, query strings, search dates, inclusion or exclusion rules, duplicate handling, screening flow, quality assessment, or extraction protocol. The bibliography is therefore a curated narrative collection rather than evidence that the field was comprehensively sampled.

key_findings.claim: The assertion that PINN training does not involve discretized temporal or spatial domains is false as stated, and the paper's own derivation explicitly uses discrete collocation sets.
key_findings.evidence: Section 2.1 says continuous PDE constraints mean training does not involve discretized grids and therefore can be highly accurate. Yet Equations 8-9 first discretize the domain and boundary into finite point sets, and Equation 14 evaluates data and residual terms at N sampled points. Automatic differentiation removes finite-difference approximation of derivatives; it does not remove finite sampling of the domain, boundary, or time interval.

key_findings.claim: The survey repeatedly presents DNN PDE methods as inherently faster or more accurate than numerical solvers without supplying resource-matched evidence, and later concedes that PINN accuracy is a principal weakness.
key_findings.evidence: Section 2 claims exponential efficiency improvement, the PINN discussion says practical use avoids FEM's iterative computations, and Section 5 calls DNN methods undoubtedly more efficient and thorough. No original benchmark, timing, training cost, amortization analysis, error tolerance, mesh resolution, or hardware comparison appears. Section 5.2 then says physics-informed methods remain less accurate than numerical methods in high-end simulation, directly qualifying the earlier general claims.

key_findings.claim: The neural-operator discussion correctly identifies amortized family-level prediction as distinct from solving one fixed instance, but overstates mesh freedom and freedom from retraining.
key_findings.evidence: DeepONet and FNO are described as learning function-to-function maps from many numerical-solver outputs and sharing behavior across a PDE family. Their displayed theorems require compact sets, continuity, and finitely sampled input functions, while practical FNO uses discretized FFT data. A trained operator avoids retraining only for parameter, forcing, geometry, resolution, or boundary variations represented by its inputs and training distribution; arbitrary changes remain out of distribution.

key_findings.claim: Universal approximation is used as conceptual motivation, but it does not establish trainability, sample complexity, stability, conservation, convergence rate, or superiority as a PDE solver.
key_findings.evidence: Theorems 1-5 are reproduced from prior function, functional, and operator approximation work under squashing-function, compactness, continuity, and finite-memory assumptions. They are existence statements. The survey moves from them to language such as laid firmly, more potent, accurately depict, and more efficiently without separating expressivity from optimization or numerical error and without deriving a PDE-specific end-to-end guarantee.

key_findings.claim: Several reproduced mathematical statements contain source-level transcription errors that prevent the exposition from being used as a reliable standalone technical reference.
key_findings.evidence: Definition 1 writes alpha=(alpha_1,...,alpha_2) in R^n rather than ending at alpha_n; the following restriction definition equates u restricted to Gamma with W rather than W applied to u. Equation 7 switches from vector x to barred x, Equation 8 uses y(x_i) while introducing y_t only afterward, and Theorems 4-5 approximate G(x)(y) even though the quantified input is u. Theorem 5 places sensor points x_i in K_2 although u is defined on K_1, so u(x_i) is not generally defined. Theorem 4's explanatory sentence also introduces c_i(f) and U absent from its statement.

key_findings.claim: The top-level two-family taxonomy is pedagogically simple but conflates distinct tasks and leaves important solver classes at the margins.
key_findings.evidence: Forward solution of one PDE, inverse parameter estimation, data assimilation, surrogate modeling, operator learning, equation discovery, and hybrid numerical acceleration have different inputs, costs, validation criteria, and generalization targets. The paper primarily files work under PDEs as constraints or neural operators, while variational and weak-form methods, Deep Ritz and energy methods, reduced-order models, learned discretizations and closures, graph or geometry-aware operators, probabilistic uncertainty, and equation discovery are scattered as applications, variants, or others rather than organized as first-class axes.

key_findings.claim: The application section is a useful citation map, not a validation that the methods work reliably in the listed engineering and medical settings.
key_findings.evidence: Table 3 and Sections 4.1-4.4 enumerate fluids, solids, heat, electromagnetism, subsurface flow, manufacturing, medicine, inverse problems, and neural-operator applications. They do not normalize PDEs, geometries, data regimes, error norms, conventional solver baselines, training and inference cost, uncertainty, extrapolation, or deployment readiness. Words such as successful, efficient, powerful, and promising therefore summarize cited reports rather than a cross-study evaluation.

key_findings.claim: The most durable forward-looking insight is the proposed combination of physics constraints with operator learning, together with explicit attention to loss design, architecture, input parameterization, and benchmark needs.
key_findings.evidence: Section 5.2 decomposes improvement into loss, network, and input choices, then highlights physics-informed DeepONet as a way to avoid generating all training labels with a conventional simulator. It also identifies accuracy, transfer across scenarios, pretraining and fine-tuning, and integration of prior and posterior information as open directions. Later surveys broaden these topics, but this paper captures the convergence early and accessibly.

key_findings.claim: The visual and structural material is broad but explanatory rather than evidentiary, and one composite figure lacks image-level provenance.
key_findings.evidence: All seven figures and three tables were inspected. Figures 1, 6, and 7 are timelines or conceptual taxonomies; Figures 2 and 4 restate PINN and DeepONet mechanisms; Figure 3 sketches supervised operator-data generation; Figure 5 is a montage of application outputs. None reports a new experiment or quantitative comparison. Figure 5 labels example domains but neither its caption nor the source identifies the provenance or license of each embedded panel, limiting visual traceability.

key_findings.claim: The paper artifact is reproducible as a document, but the review process and its substantive conclusions are not reproducible from released artifacts.
key_findings.evidence: The official arXiv source package contains the main TeX, IEEE class, a 318-entry BibTeX library, the rendered 222-item bibliography, seven used composite figures plus unused alternatives, and author images. It compiles successfully in two pdfLaTeX passes on a current TeX Live installation. It contains no environment lock because none is needed for analysis, but also no search log, screening decisions, extraction table, quality ratings, quantitative synthesis, code, or data with which to reconstruct Tables 1-3 or audit study selection.

method.core_idea: Organize roughly four decades of neural approaches to differential equations around physics constraints and neural operators, trace their approximation-theory ancestry, and map them to scientific, engineering, medical, and inverse-problem applications.
method.mechanism: The paper narrates a timeline from Hopfield minimization through function and operator universal approximation, reproduces representative equations and theorems for Lagaris networks, PINNs, DeepONet, and FNO, groups cited applications in tables, and proposes a loss-network-input framework for future improvements and hybrid physics-informed operators.
assumptions: The selected 1982-2022 literature is representative even though no search or screening protocol is reported.
PDE-constrained networks and neural operators are sufficient principal categories for the field.
Universal approximation results provide useful foundations for practical PDE learning despite not guaranteeing optimization or numerical performance.
Published application reports can support broad field-level conclusions without standardized cross-study metrics.
Amortized inference benefits of learned surrogates can be discussed separately from their data-generation and training costs.
The paper is a narrative survey and does not claim a new algorithm, dataset, benchmark, or empirical result.

techniques.role: Represent the PDE, initial conditions, boundary conditions, and observations as terms or constructions governing neural-network training.
Learn maps between input and output function spaces for amortized prediction across a parameterized PDE family.
Connect feed-forward, functional, and operator networks to universal approximation existence results.
Evaluate PDE residual derivatives of neural solutions without finite-difference derivative formulas.
Cross-reference methods with physical domains, engineering and medical use, and inverse problems.
Trace conceptual links from early neural minimization and function approximation to PINNs, DeepONet, and FNO.

evaluations.result: The rendered bibliography contains 222 entries spanning 1982-2022, and Tables 1-3 distribute citations across theory, method, application, inverse problems, and future perspectives.
evaluations.baseline: No systematic search protocol, competing survey corpus, or recall estimate is supplied.

evaluations.result: The main text contains 18 numbered equations, five reproduced theorems, one corollary, and three definitions, but multiple notation and domain errors occur in Definitions 1-2, Equations 7-8, and Theorems 4-5.
evaluations.baseline: The cited original theorem and method papers, whose exact statements should be consulted instead.

evaluations.result: The survey covers fluid, solid, heat, electromagnetism, subsurface, manufacturing, medical, inverse, and operator-learning applications through narrative citations.
evaluations.baseline: No common accuracy, compute, data, robustness, uncertainty, or deployment metric is extracted across studies.

evaluations.result: No original experiment or quantitative synthesis tests the general efficiency and accuracy claims for PINNs or neural operators.
evaluations.baseline: FDM, FEM, conventional CFD, and other numerical methods are discussed rhetorically rather than compared at matched error and total cost.

evaluations.result: The official arXiv e-print source compiled successfully in two pdfLaTeX passes to a 20-page PDF in a current TeX Live environment.
evaluations.baseline: The fresh official PDF is byte-identical to the pinned cache; the locally rebuilt PDF is not byte-identical because the source does not pin the historical TeX environment.

evaluations.result: All seven figures and three tables were inspected; they are conceptual diagrams, taxonomies, citation tables, or application illustrations rather than new measured results.
evaluations.baseline: No plotted benchmark, uncertainty interval, ablation, or statistical synthesis is present.

limitations: No reproducible literature-search, screening, extraction, or quality-assessment protocol is reported.
The comprehensive-review claim is not supported by a coverage or recall analysis.
The top-level taxonomy reduces a multi-axis field to physics constraints and neural operators.
PDE solution, inverse inference, data assimilation, surrogate prediction, equation discovery, and numerical-solver augmentation are not cleanly separated.
Statements that PINNs avoid spatial or temporal discretization ignore finite collocation and boundary sampling.
Statements that neural methods are inherently or exponentially more efficient lack matched total-cost evidence.
Training cost, numerical data generation, hyperparameter search, amortization horizon, and inference cost are not jointly analyzed.
Accuracy claims are not tied to PDE-specific norms, tolerances, conservation defects, or conventional-solver baselines.
Universal approximation existence theorems are treated too closely as practical performance foundations.
The theorem exposition contains variable, domain, and restriction transcription errors.
The FNO definition suppresses practical discretization, mode truncation, aliasing, boundary, and geometry constraints.
Neural-operator no-retraining claims omit dependence on the parameterization and training distribution.
The application survey does not distinguish proof-of-concept demonstrations from validated or deployed systems.
Uncertainty quantification, out-of-distribution behavior, stiffness, multiscale spectral bias, optimization pathologies, and failure detection receive limited treatment.
No benchmark table normalizes datasets, PDEs, metrics, hardware, code availability, or reproducibility.
Figure 5 does not provide image-level source or license attribution for its embedded application panels.
The review corpus and table assignments cannot be reconstructed from released artifacts.
There is no appendix, supplementary audit, code repository, or data artifact supporting the review process.
failure_modes: A reader may interpret automatic differentiation as eliminating domain discretization rather than only derivative discretization.
A reader may compare cheap neural inference against the full runtime of a numerical solver while omitting training and label-generation cost.
A universal approximation theorem may be mistaken for a convergence, stability, or learnability guarantee.
A neural operator may fail after changing geometry, coefficients, boundary conditions, forcing, or resolution outside its training support.
Soft residual minimization can produce a low sampled loss while missing localized PDE, boundary, conservation, or stability errors.
Broad application counts may be mistaken for cross-domain evidence of reliability or industrial readiness.
Theorem transcription errors can propagate incorrect sensor domains or undefined expressions into secondary explanations.
A two-family taxonomy can hide hybrid solvers, variational formulations, learned discretizations, closures, and equation discovery.
Qualitative words such as efficient and successful can erase differences in error tolerance, hardware, data, and amortization regime.
Without a screening log, citation selection can overrepresent positive results and underrepresent failures or conventional baselines.
reusable_insights: Separate instance solvers from amortized solution-operator learners before comparing cost or transfer.
Distinguish derivative discretization, domain sampling, representation discretization, and solver iteration explicitly.
Treat universal approximation as an expressivity result, then audit optimization, sampling, stability, and error separately.
Compare total offline plus online cost at a fixed accuracy and an explicit number of downstream queries.
Organize neural PDE work along task, physics incorporation, representation, supervision, geometry, uncertainty, and deployment axes rather than one method axis.
Physics-informed operator learning can reduce labeled-simulator dependence while retaining family-level prediction, but still requires coverage and error control.
A useful survey artifact should release queries, screening decisions, extraction fields, study-quality judgments, and benchmark normalization.
Application breadth is best treated as a research map until matched baselines and reliability evidence are available.
open_questions: Which neural PDE methods beat modern numerical solvers in end-to-end cost at matched error, including training and data generation?
How should benchmark suites expose conservation error, long-horizon instability, stiffness, multiscale behavior, geometry shift, and out-of-distribution failure?
What assumptions convert operator approximation into finite-sample, optimization, discretization, and deployment guarantees?
When do physics residuals improve generalization rather than create ill-conditioned multi-objective optimization?
How can neural operators adapt safely to unseen coefficients, forcings, boundaries, meshes, and geometries with calibrated uncertainty?
Which hybrid designs most effectively augment rather than replace mature numerical solvers?
How should surveys distinguish forward solution, inverse inference, discovery, emulation, closure learning, and solver acceleration?
Would a reproducible re-screening of the 1982-2022 corpus materially change the paper's two-family taxonomy or application conclusions?

competitive_landscape.title: Physics-informed machine learning
competitive_landscape.relationship: A direct prior review of physics-informed learning, operator regression, forward and inverse problems, applications, limitations, and benchmark needs.
competitive_landscape.difference: It is narrower than Huang et al.'s four-decade neural-PDE history but offers a more explicit physics-data integration framework and limitations agenda. Because it appeared in 2021 and is cited by the reviewed paper, the claim that a comprehensive review was still lacking must be read as a claim about the authors' broader taxonomy, not absence of major reviews.

competitive_landscape.title: Scientific Machine Learning through Physics-Informed Neural Networks: Where we are and What's next
competitive_landscape.relationship: A direct prior PINN survey covering vanilla, conservative, variational, and other collocation-based variants, their applications, advantages, disadvantages, and unresolved theory.
competitive_landscape.difference: Cuomo et al. is narrower because it does not center neural operators, but it gives a more detailed PINN method taxonomy and a more candid limitations treatment. It was current before Huang et al.'s submission and further weakens any literal no-comprehensive-review claim.

competitive_landscape.title: Machine Learning for Partial Differential Equations
competitive_landscape.relationship: A later broad review of machine learning for PDE discovery, reduced coordinates and models, solution operators, and improvement of traditional numerical algorithms.
competitive_landscape.difference: Brunton and Kutz organize the field by scientific task rather than mainly by PINNs versus neural operators, so they cover discovery and numerical augmentation more centrally and avoid presenting neural methods as a single replacement paradigm.

competitive_landscape.title: A Survey on Solving and Discovering Differential Equations Using Deep Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: A later DNN-DE survey that explicitly separates solving from discovery, proposes an application taxonomy, and supplies a DeepXDE tutorial.
competitive_landscape.difference: Jung et al. is less centered on operator learning but is more reproducible pedagogically because it demonstrates a concrete forward and inverse transport-equation workflow. Its task distinction repairs one of Huang et al.'s principal taxonomic conflations.

competitive_landscape.title: From PINNs to PIKANs: Recent Advances in Physics-Informed Machine Learning
competitive_landscape.relationship: A current review of PINN architecture, feature expansion, adaptive refinement, domain decomposition, optimization, uncertainty, applications, and software.
competitive_landscape.difference: It is substantially narrower than the historical PINN-plus-operator scope, but much more current and technically granular about why PINNs train poorly and how later architectures and tooling address those problems.

competitive_landscape.title: Adaptive Physics-informed Neural Networks: A Survey
competitive_landscape.relationship: A focused current survey of transfer-learning and meta-learning approaches for PINN convergence and rapid adaptation across PDE parameters.
competitive_landscape.difference: It directly addresses the re-optimization limitation that Huang et al. identify but sometimes obscure with broad claims about neural transfer. Its scope is specialized, while its problem statement is more precise about when a PINN must be retrained.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim the missing comprehensive review of DNN methods for PDEs, offering a common taxonomy, a four-decade history, mathematical foundations, applications, and future directions.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper does combine early Hopfield computation, function and functional approximation, PINNs, DeepONet, FNO, application tables, and a physics-data convergence perspective in one 20-page survey.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The synthesis is broad and accessible but only moderately novel: major prior reviews already covered physics-informed machine learning and PINNs, and no systematic-review evidence supports comprehensiveness. Its distinctive value is the compact historical bridge from early neural computation to the paired PINN/operator taxonomy and the early emphasis on physics-informed operators, not a definitive technical or empirical account.

reviewer_notes: Exact-source audit used the pinned 20-page arXiv v2 PDF and extracted text. Local PDF/text hashes match the full-text index, and a fresh official arXiv PDF downloaded on 2026-08-24 was byte-identical; the official record remains v2, revised 2022-11-18. Every page was rendered and inspected, covering seven figures, three tables, 18 numbered equations, five theorems, one corollary, three definitions, all 222 rendered references, and no appendices or original experiments. The PDF title lists six authors although the current arXiv metadata lists four; the later IEEE TNNLS publication lists all six, but the pinned arXiv artifact was not replaced. The official e-print package (SHA-256 ee1a579db77d4c3f6ceec2ac9adc787f5f8ea3e7ba465a4e9dc2c75b54318425) contains TeX, the IEEE class, a 318-entry BibTeX file, the 222-item BBL, composite figures, unused alternatives, and author images; it compiled successfully in two pdfLaTeX passes on current TeX Live to 20 pages. No first-party code, dataset, search log, screening record, extraction sheet, or review-quality rubric was found or claimed. Six direct prior or later reviews were revision-checked against primary publisher or arXiv records through 2026-08-24.
